candidats.titre: Synthetic controls meet Lucas! Unifying causal effects and structural decompositions
candidats.resume: This paper merges two large literatures in macroeconomics, Synthetic Control Method (SCM) and Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) models, into a single framework. SCM effectively estimates causal treatment effects but lacks insights into underlying economic mechanisms, and it does not offer a framework for policy analysis: its estimated effect is a reduced-form object that shifts with the policy regime, leaving it exposed to the Lucas critique. By integrating SCM outcomes into a micro-founded DSGE framework, representing the treatment as an observable event that loads on the model’s structural shocks, we identify the transmission channels underlying the SCM-estimated treatment effects and enhance structural interpretation. Our approach recovers policy-invariant structural primitives rather than the regime-dependent gap, enabling counterfactual policy analysis that is robust to the Lucas critique. It thereby unites the empirical transparency of synthetic controls with the structural discipline of DSGE models – two complementary literatures that have long developed in isolation.

candidats.titre: The Effects of Private Plan Subsidies on Enrollment: Evidence from Medicare Advantage -- by Paul D. Jacobs, Timothy J. Layton
candidats.resume: Some social insurance programs, including the Medicare program in the United States, allow beneficiaries to choose between public and private insurance firms. In these types of programs, the government will often provide a voucher to those who opt for private firms. A key policy decision is the level of this voucher, and a key input to that decision is the elasticity of enrollment in the public versus the private option with respect to the size of the voucher. We estimate this elasticity in the Medicare program, where recent work has provided remarkably little evidence on how Medicare Advantage (MA) enrollment responds to payment despite the program’s rapid growth. We leverage the fact that the formula determining county-level “benchmark” payments (vouchers) involves coarse thresholds based on county-level spending and counties occasionally move across these thresholds, providing a shock to the vouchers unrelated to beneficiary demand. Using several complementary estimation strategies, we find that a 1 percent increase in a county’s benchmark raises MA enrollment by roughly half a percentage point within three years, implying an elasticity of about 2. Applying this estimate to a policy counterfactual that sets benchmarks at 95 percent of county fee-for-service spending implies a decline in MA enrollment of about 6.1 percentage points, or roughly one-quarter of our sample. We also provide suggestive evidence, consistent with prior work, that the increase in benchmarks gets passed through in the form of additional benefits, providing a mechanism for the enrollment increases.

candidats.titre: How AI Impacts the Quest for Knowledge: Evidence from AlphaFold2 -- by Myra Mohnen, Joshua S. Gans
candidats.resume: Scientists can respond to artificial intelligence by pushing the frontier of science and asking new questions, or by deepening their understanding of questions already studied. We study how AI shapes this choice in structural biology, where experiments examine a protein's three-dimensional structure and its function. AlphaFold2, released in 2021, predicts the structure of almost every known protein, with a confidence that varies across proteins. Linking 530,471 proteins to the experiments run on them between 2017 and 2025, we compare how experimental activity changed after 2021 across proteins with more and less confident predictions. Where predictions are more confident, the experimental record adds fewer first structures for proteins far from any relative of known structure. It adds more follow-up experiments on proteins whose structure is already known, and the rise is largest for proteins surrounded by relatives of known structure. A model of experimental choice shows how AlphaFold2 can deepen existing knowledge rather than extend it: a prediction replaces an experiment that would establish a protein's structure, and it lowers the cost of experiments that build on that structure.

candidats.titre: Valuing the Cost of Incomplete Global Markets -- by Karen K. Lewis, Edith X. Liu
candidats.resume: Deviations from complete financial markets in cross-border investments generate economic welfare costs. This paper shows how to value these costs using standard theory and data based on three main results. Our first result shows how welfare valuations can be derived from a general wealth-to-dividend ratio. Next, we establish how aggregate consumption and exchange rate data can be used to uncover diversifiable goods allocations across countries. Finally, we demonstrate how asset pricing data and models can be used to value deviations from complete markets. The paper outlines a range of applications that fall under this framework, including financial intermediary constraint models.

candidats.titre: Are Revealed Preferences All You Need for AI Alignment? -- by Joshua S. Gans, Richard T. Holden
candidats.resume: AI agents learn what principals want from what principals choose. We offer a criterion for when a principal's decisions, at every belief an AI might hold, are all the AI needs. For acting, they are. Cautious actions, such as deferring to a person, typically divide the principal's actions into blocks, and for choosing costless evidence, decisions are enough exactly when the same evidence is best in every block. Otherwise, the AI acts as its principal would yet can gather the wrong evidence, and greater capability can turn that error into incorrect actions. Choices between two mistakes reveal what decisions miss.

Sans nouveau modèle de piège, cette méthode peu coûteuse pourrait améliorer la dératisation comme le suivi de la faune. Vous êtes-vous déjà demandé pourquoi les restaurants inscrivent à leur carte des bouteilles de vin à des prix exorbitants ? Souvent, on ne s’attend pas à ce que ces bouteilles se vendent. Elles servent plutôt à faire paraître les autres vins d’un meilleur rapport qualité-prix, même s’ils restent trop chers. En modifiant le contexte de la décision, l’option coûteuse et hors de portée peut inciter les clients à désirer davantage l’option moins chère. Les spécialistes du marketing utilisent des astuces similaires tout le temps. Un séjour de vacances affiché complet, un abonnement haut de gamme dont personne ne veut vraiment ou un produit manifestement trop cher peuvent tous influencer la façon dont nous percevons les autres choix proposés à côté. Les économistes comportementaux appellent ces influences des « effets de leurre » ( decoy effects ). Ils révèlent que les décisions ne sont pas toujours rationnelles ni fondées sur une valeur absolue. Elles sont plutôt souvent façonnées par les options disponibles à ce moment-là. À lire aussi : Soldes : les commerçants sont-ils d’honnêtes manipulateurs ? Les humains ne sont pas les seuls animaux à prendre des décisions. Chaque jour, les animaux sauvages soupèsent les risques et les bénéfices…

SAP plans to cut at least 10,000 jobs as it pivots to AI
SAP is preparing to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as part of a sweeping AI restructuring, Bloomberg reports, citing people familiar with the matter. That's at least nine percent of the company's global workforce of more than 110,000. Every department has been asked to identify savings, with product development, engineering, and sales taking the biggest hit. The final number hasn't been set and could change after negotiations with employee representatives.
In Germany, where about a quarter of SAP's workforce is based, a job guarantee runs through 2028. CEO Christian Klein wants to embed AI tools across SAP's product lineup. The company already cut roughly 10,000 jobs in 2024. Its competitors are making similar moves. Oracle slashed 21,000 positions over twelve months, and Microsoft is offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees. SAP declined to comment on the potential cuts, saying only that it reviews its organizational structure on an ongoing basis. The company recently announced a partnership with Mistral AI and has acquired several startups.

OpenAI is suing Apple for trade secret theft and unfair business practices. The ChatGPT maker filed the lawsuit Friday in a California court, the Financial Times reports. The company also alleges that Apple encourages employees to store corporate data on personal devices, then turns that practice against staff who want to leave. According to the complaint, a former OpenAI employee passed along details about product plans and suppliers after returning to Apple.
The countersuit follows Apple's own lawsuit from the summer, which accused several former employees of leaking confidential information to OpenAI. The AI company had previously closed its $6.4 billion acquisition of former Apple chief designer Jony Ive's studio "io" and is preparing its own devices to rival Apple. Vendredi noir, et même très noir, pour la France que ce 27 novembre. Récession, déficit accru, inquiétude concernant la dette : en ce « Black Friday », les mauvaises nouvelles économiques et budgétaires sont tombées dru. Ensemble, elles montrent qu’au lieu de se redresser, comme en rêvait le gouvernement, le pays s’enfonce plutôt dans la crise. S&P Global Ratings, la principale agence mondiale de notation, a clos la journée par un avertissement frappant : si la situation ne s’améliore pas, la société américaine envisage d’abaisser la note qu’elle attribue à la dette française.
S&P, qui évalue la capacité des entreprises et des pays à rembourser leurs emprunts, a maintenu dans l’immédiat sa note A+, correspondant à une dette de qualité « moyenne supérieure ». L’équivalent d’un 15,5 sur 20 pour une copie scolaire. Cependant, l’agence a revu la perspective qu’elle accole à cette évaluation, de « stable » à « négative ». Ce qui ouvre la voie à une possible dégradation de la note lors du prochain examen par S&P, en principe dans quelques mois.
La France se trouve ainsi confrontée à une triple menace. Moody’s et Fitch, les deux grandes agences concurrentes de S&P, ont, en effet, déjà assorti d’une perspective négative les notes qu’elles accordent à la dette tricolore.

L'agence de notation Standard & Poor's menace de dégrader prochainement la note de la France
Cette décision s'explique notamment par des perspectives de croissance en berne pour la dette française.
Un résultat très attendu, alors que les députés sont toujours en pleins débats budgétaires. L'agence de notation S&P Global a maintenu, vendredi 27 novembre, la note de la France à A+, mais a abaissé la perspective de stable à négative, la menaçant donc d'une dégradation, en raison des difficultés du pays à réduire son déficit.
Le ministre de l'Economie, Roland Lescure, a "pris acte" de cette évaluation, estimant qu'elle venait "souligner l'absolue nécessité de doter le pays dans les meilleurs délais d'un budget responsable, qui redresse nos finances publiques en ramenant le déficit à 5% au plus".
En mai, S&P Global avait maintenu la note de la dette souveraine française, qui évalue la capacité du pays à rembourser ses emprunts, à A+. Autrement dit, l'agence considérait alors la dette comme étant de qualité "moyenne supérieure", avec perspective stable.
La croissance française en berne
Avant la publication de cette note, certains économistes prédisaient un abaissement de la dette française par S&P. A l'instar d'Eric Dor, directeur des études économiques à l'école de commerce Ieseg, qui rappelait que S&P disposait "des arguments pour" abaisser la note de la France. En octobre 2025, l'agence misait sur une croissance de 1% pour 2026 pour l'économie française. Or ce scénario est désormais totalement hors d'atteinte, avec un produit intérieur brut (PIB) en recul de 0,2 % au premier trimestre, stable au deuxième et en nouveau recul de 0,1 % au troisième.
Toutefois, cette prédiction ne faisait pas l'unanimité. Anthony Morlet-Lavidalie, économiste à Rexecode, interrogé par l'AFP, estimait "assez violent" une rétrogradation de la note d'un cran. "Le scénario le plus logique", prédisait-il, serait un simple abaissement de la perspective, voire également un statu quo en attendant de voir si un budget 2027 finit par être adopté au parlement. Avis partagé par Stéphane Colliac, économiste de BNP Paribas. "S&P n'a pas une obligation de dégrader la note" dès maintenant, d'autant que "la situation budgétaire reste plus incertaine que négative", estimait-il.

Budget 2027 : après quelques couacs, le Sénat s’apprête à revoter sur la fiscalisation des ALD et la suppression de la demi-part fiscale des mères célibataires
Les sénateurs vont jouer les prolongations, ce week-end, sur la première partie du budget 2027. La Chambre haute, qui débat depuis une semaine du volet « recettes » du projet de loi de finances pour 2027 (PLF), devrait arriver au bout de la discussion en séance publique dimanche. Mais avant le vote sur cette partie du texte, les élus ont prévu de remettre aux voix deux dispositions polémiques, adoptées cette semaine avec l’article 2 du PLF : l’imposition des indemnités liées à une affection de longue durée (ALD) et la suppression d’une niche fiscale en faveur des mères célibataires.
Le groupe Les Républicains a annoncé demander cette deuxième délibération afin de voter à nouveau deux mesures qui, en l’état, « impacteraient injustement deux catégories de personnes en situation de fragilité ». La première concerne les affections longue durées. Mercredi, le Sénat, à l’initiative de la rapporteure générale du budget, la sénatrice LR Christine Lavarde, a adopté une taxation totale des indemnités liées à une ALD, quand le gouvernement souhaitait une imposition sur la moitié de leur montant.
Autre mesure polémique qui doit faire l’objet d’un second débat : la suppression de la demi-part fiscale supplémentaire pour les mères célibataires. Là encore à l’initiative de la rapporteure, les élus ont fait sauter lundi la demi-part de quotient accordée à vie aux mères qui ont élevé seules, pendant au moins cinq ans, un ou plusieurs enfants, une disposition instaurée en 1945 pour soutenir les veuves de guerre.
« Les LR se sont renduscompte qu’ils ont fait une bêtise »
L’article 43 du règlement de la Haute Assemblée permet de remettre aux voix certains articles d’un projet ou d’une proposition de loi, juste avant le vote sur l’ensemble du texte. À condition que cette seconde délibération ait été demandée, ou acceptée, soit par le gouvernement, soit par la commission saisie du texte.
Le vote de ces deux mesures, grâce aux voix de la majorité sénatoriale de droite et du centre, contre l’avis du gouvernement, a été motivé par un contexte de forte disette budgétaire. En début de semaine, le Premier ministre a adressé un courrier aux parlementaires pour leur demander de dégager six milliards d’euros d’économies supplémentaires, en plus des 43 milliards d’euros déjà compris dans le projet de loi initiale, du fait des révisions à la baisse des prévisions de croissance pour l’année prochaine.
« Les LR se sont rendu compte qu’ils ont fait une bêtise. Les gens concernés sont montés au créneau. J’avais moi-même indiqué en séance que ces mesures étaient disproportionnées et néfastes », explique le sénateur Les Indépendants Emmanuel Capus. Ce proche d’Edouard Philippe réclame notamment la défiscalisation totale des ALD. « Nous avons une situation financière compliquée, mais sur ces sujets, notre regard doit être humain plutôt que budgétaire », défend-il. « Et puis, ce sont des augmentations déguisées d’impôts, ce à quoi nous sommes fermement opposés. »
Les niches fiscales dans le viseur de la commission
La taxation des ALD et la suppression de la demi-part fiscale des mères célibataires a également soulevé un véritable tollé dans les rangs des oppositions de gauche. En séance, Patrick Kanner, le président du groupe socialiste, est allé jusqu’à qualifier de « dégueulasse » l’amendement de la rapporteure sur les affections longue durée. Dans un post sur son compte X, l’élu du Nord, a également raillé « la cacophonie » au sein de la majorité sénatoriale, puisque ce sont les LR qui demandent cette seconde délibération, après avoir voté ces articles, modifiés par la rapporteure, qui est elle-même issue des rangs de la droite.
« Elle s’est lancée dans une sorte d’inventaire de toutes les sources d’économies possibles, et cherche à faire supprimer les dispositions dérogatoires, parfois sans distinction. Or, il faut garder à l’esprit que, souvent, ces niches sont là pour compenser certaines situations », commente Emmanuel Capus.

a37.texte:
Auditionné sur le budget du ministère de la Justice, Gérald Darmanin se félicite de crédits en hausse de 420 millions d’euros pour 2027, pour atteindre quasiment 11 milliards d’euros. « Depuis 10 ans, les crédits du ministère de la Justice ont augmenté de 61 % », souligne le ministre. Concernant la loi intégrale, les « premiers crédits » sont prévus dans le budget, mais il faudra un projet de loi de finances rectificative pour aller au bout, prévient le garde des Sceaux.
La proposition de loi mettant fin au devoir conjugal en passe d’être définitivement adoptée par le Parlement
Le 23 janvier dernier, une femme de 69 ans a ainsi été jugée fautive dans son divorce pour avoir refusé des rapports sexuels à son mari. Une « violation grave et renouvelée des devoirs du mariage, » avait tranché la justice. Si le devoir conjugal en tant que tel n’est donc pas inscrit dans la loi, il était encore au cœur d’une quinzaine d’arrêts d’appel en 2025. La même année, la France a été sanctionnée par la Cour européenne des droits de l’homme (CEDH) pour ce motif, lui imposant d’abandonner la jurisprudence.
Il y a presque un an, la députée écologiste Marie-Charlotte Garin disait qu’il serait anormal « que le mariage soit le dernier lieu dans lequel le consentement n’aurait pas sa place », après la condamnation de la France par l’instance européenne. Dans le Code civil, quatre devoirs liés au mariage sont clairement établis : le secours, la fidélité, l’assistance, et la communauté de vie. Le devoir conjugal, lui, n’est pas mentionné. Mais, dans la jurisprudence, la rédaction de l’article 242 portant sur les motifs des divorces pour faute a pu conduire à considérer que la « communauté de vie » mentionnée impliquait une forme de « devoir conjugal ».
La proposition de loi, portée à l’Assemblée nationale par les députés Marie-Charlotte Garin (Ecologistes) et Paul Christophe (Horizons), est soutenue par le gouvernement. La ministre déléguée à l’égalité entre les femmes et les hommes Aurore Bergé a notamment exprimé en avril dernier qu’il fallait « mettre en cohérence » le droit français avec la condamnation européenne.
Un vote unanime
Le 9 avril, la proposition de loi avait été adoptée au Sénat, au terme de longues discussions sémantiques portant sur la rédaction de l’article 1er, modifié par rapport à la version initiale de l’Assemblée, et sur la suppression de l’article 2. L’article en question statuait que le divorce « ne peut être fondé sur l’absence ou le refus de relations sexuelles, » ce que les sénateurs avaient vu comme une redite avec l’objet même de la proposition de loi. Pour le rapporteur de la proposition au Sénat, Jean-Baptiste Blanc (Les Républicains), il n’y avait « pas d’utilité juridique » à adopter cette disposition. Le texte a ensuite été adopté à l’unanimité par la chambre haute, à 209 voix pour et 2 contre.
Le désaccord persistant entre l’Assemblée nationale et le Sénat sur la rédaction de la proposition de loi, il appartenait à une commission mixte paritaire (CMP) de trancher sur le texte final qui sera soumis au vote du Parlement. Finalement, les sept représentants de chaque chambre se sont accordés à l’unanimité pour conserver l’article 1 dans la version initiale telle que votée par l’Assemblée nationale. En guise de compromis, l’article 2 de la proposition de loi a été supprimé, conformément au vote du Sénat.
« Même dans le mariage, le consentement n’est jamais acquis, » a tenu à rappeler à l’issue du vote la rapporteure Marie-Charlotte Garin. Le texte s’inscrit dans la continuité juridique de l’intégration du non-consentement dans la définition pénale du viol et des agressions sexuelles, une proposition de loi que la députée avait également portée, jusqu’à son adoption le 23 octobre 2025.
Au terme de la réunion de la commission mixte paritaire conclusive, le texte abrogeant le devoir conjugal doit encore être voté par les deux chambres du Parlement. Une procédure accélérée a été enclenchée par le gouvernement sur ce texte, et le soutien transpartisan dont il fait l’objet doit permettre son vote rapide. Le texte fera d’abord son entrée au Palais Bourbon le 7 décembre. La date de l’examen du texte par le Sénat, n’a, elle, pas encore été définie.
Chloé Auffray

Taiwan is choosing mayors, council members and other local leaders across its 22 cities and counties in an election that has been unusually competitive in some of the island’s biggest cities.
Polls opened at 8am (00:00 GMT) on Saturday and will close at 4pm (08:00 GMT), with results expected early in the evening.
Voters are casting ballots at schools, temples and community centres.
About 11,000 positions are at stake in the “nine-in-one” elections, named for the nine categories of local government posts being contested.
Taipei mayoral race
A key contest is for the mayor of the capital, Taipei, a traditional stronghold of the opposition Kuomintang (KMT).
Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the KMT, who won by a double-digit margin in the last election and is seen as a possible future presidential candidate, faces a strong challenge from Puma Shen of the governing Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).
Shen is an academic-turned-lawmaker and an expert on China’s information warfare. China has denounced him, and Chinese police say he is wanted for “separatism”. He entered the race as the underdog, but has drawn huge crowds at his rallies.
Shen’s victory in the KMT’s heartland could be seen as “quite shameful” in Beijing, said Austin Wang, a political scientist at the University of Nevada.
Chiang told supporters the race was “very close”.
Shen cancelled a final rally over traffic concerns and held an online event instead, which drew more than 500,000 viewers on YouTube. President William Lai Ching-te of the DPP also urged voters at a rally in neighbouring New Taipei City to back the party’s candidates there.
Other notable races are in New Taipei City, Taiwan’s most populous city, and Kaohsiung, in the south. New Taipei City’s incumbent mayor is from the KMT, while Kaohsiung’s mayoral office is held by the DPP.
China’s pressure
The vote will not directly change Taiwan’s China policy, and campaigns have focused on local issues such as transport, childcare and the environment.
Beijing, which claims Taiwan as its own territory, has repeatedly weighed in, and the vote is being closely watched there.
Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense counted some 33 sorties from China’s People’s Liberation Army warplanes between Friday and Saturday flying toward Taiwan, including bombers and fighter jets.
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council has warned that Beijing is trying to influence the outcome through “cognitive warfare” and “transnational repression”.
China’s Defence Ministry said this week that “reunification” is an unstoppable trend.
In the last local elections four years ago, the KMT won 14 cities and counties, the DPP five and other parties or independents three. The KMT traditionally favours closer ties with Beijing, while the DPP rejects China’s sovereignty claims.
Analysts say local results are an unreliable guide to the outcome of the next presidential election, due in early 2028. Lai is expected to seek a second term.
The KMT could begin debating its presidential ticket soon after the vote. The likely candidates include outgoing Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen and parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu.
KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun, who met Chinese President Xi Jinping in April, is also seen as a possible challenger, though she could face pressure to step down if the party does badly.

Du 21 au 27 novembre à 14h, la revue a recensé 32 actions hostiles visant l’Europe, survenues récemment ou rendues publiques ces derniers jours. Dix-huit sont attribuées à la Russie ou soupçonnées de l’être, et aucun auteur n’a encore été désigné pour les quatorze autres.
Il s’agit de la semaine la plus chargée depuis le début du recensement, fin septembre : c’est trois fois la moyenne d’octobre, et 10 de plus que la semaine précédente (22).
- On compte ainsi douze incidents aériens, dix opérations d’espionnage, deux campagnes de désinformation, une vague de fausses alertes à la bombe, un projet d’assassinat, un drone marin chargé d’explosifs, l’implantation d’une cellule hacktiviste prorusse, deux affaires d’incendies criminels visant l’industrie de défense, une cyberattaque et un brouillage GPS.
- L’Est du continent a été le plus touché : 23 des 32 actions visent des pays de la frontière orientale, de la Baltique à la mer Noire. La Pologne figure en tête (6), devant la Roumanie (5). Les trois pays baltes en comptent 8 à eux trois.
- À l’inverse, aucune action n’a visé le Royaume-Uni ni les Pays-Bas cette semaine.
La majeure partie de ces événements (20 sur 32) correspondent à des actions ou à des affaires survenues au cours des semaines, des mois, voire des années précédentes, mais qui ont été révélées ou recensées ces derniers jours, souvent à l’occasion d’une arrestation, d’un procès ou d’une enquête. Douze actions se sont produites pendant la période, soit à peu près autant que les deux semaines précédentes (11 et 12).
Ainsi, en Pologne, deux affaires antérieures ont émergé cette semaine.
- Jeudi 26 novembre, le tribunal de Bydgoszcz a condamné à trois ans de prison un pianiste, arrêté en juin 2025, qui s’était proposé au renseignement russe et avait transmis des informations sur des sites militaires à un contact qu’il croyait du FSB. Celui-ci s’est révélé être un agent du contre-espionnage polonais.
- Le 24 novembre, deux ressortissants serbes ont été identifiés comme suspects de l’incendie criminel qui avait visé fin août l’usine du fabricant de drones militaires WB Electronics, à Skarżysko-Kamienna. Ils ont quitté la Pologne et font l’objet d’un mandat d’arrêt européen. Donald Tusk avait qualifié l’incendie « d’acte de sabotage ».
Les affaires d’espionnage ont atteint un niveau inédit cette semaine, avec dix actions recensées, dont neuf attribuées à la Russie ou soupçonnées de l’être, contre trois au maximum les semaines précédentes.
- En Estonie, le Service de sécurité intérieure (Kaitsepolitseiamet, ou KAPO) a fait expulser deux ressortissants russes dont il dit les liens avec le renseignement russe établis. Il s’agit d’un ancien professeur et journaliste, qui renseignait les services de Moscou sur la population russophone, et d’un employé de l’usine d’huile de schiste d’Enefit, à Auvere, expulsé le 24 novembre.
- En Lituanie, le parquet a annoncé le 25 novembre l’interpellation de cinq personnes soupçonnées de collecter des informations contre rémunération, depuis l’automne 2024, pour la télévision d’État russe VGTRK. Des institutions lituaniennes disent avoir reçu de plusieurs d’entre eux des centaines de questions, notamment sur la défense aérienne et l’OTAN.
- En Allemagne, deux procès pour espionnage au profit de la Russie se sont ouverts le 26 novembre : à Düsseldorf, l’accusé a avoué avoir espionné pour le FSB un homme lié à l’armée ukrainienne, tandis qu’à Berlin, une Germano-Ukrainienne est accusée d’avoir signalé des réunions politiques de haut niveau à un agent russe en poste à l’ambassade.
Les pays de l’Est du continent ont désigné la Russie plus souvent que les autres cette semaine.
- Une autorité de ces pays l’a fait pour plus de la moitié des actions qui les visent (12 sur 23), contre seulement 2 sur 9 à l’Ouest.
- L’écart tient surtout à la Pologne, aux pays baltes et à la Finlande, où gouvernements, services de sécurité et parquets mettent régulièrement en cause Moscou.
Pour suivre au jour le jour la guerre politique russe contre l’Europe, notre Observatoire est mis à jour quotidiennement à partir des dernières informations.

Trump effectively ended asylum. Advocates look to the Supreme Court to restore it
For nearly two years, the Trump administration has prohibited asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border, canceled thousands of pending asylum applications and overhauled the immigration court system with mass firings. Critics say that combined, these moves have effectively shut down a once vital pathway for those fleeing persecution or danger.
The U.S. Supreme Court will soon consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections.
The legal challenge to the president's ban, which went into effect within hours of President Trump retaking office, is the latest legal case against the administration's seismic immigration policy changes that will be taken up by the high court. Those policy changes, critics say, have robbed asylum seekers of basic due process rights and have transformed the immigration court system into a deportation arm of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
In legal filings, the Trump administration has insisted the proclamation is a necessary protection against "invasion" along the southern border and what the president and conservative critics have long said is abuse of the system by "fake" asylum seekers. Since it has been in place, the chaotic crush of people crossing into the U.S. has plummeted. U.S. Border Patrol apprehensions dropped to their lowest level in agency history this year. The agency recorded fewer than 99,000 Southwest border apprehensions in fiscal year 2026 — a 95% decline compared with more than 1.8 million per year under President Biden, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data.
"The difference between an average month under Trump and an average month under Biden is just staggering," Simon Hankinson, a senior research fellow with the Border Security and Immigration Center at the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank closely aligned with Trump, told NPR. And should the Supreme Court reverse the ban, "it would be disastrous," he added.
Hankinson contends that most people arriving at the southern border don't qualify for asylum. "And even if they did, they've already passed through Mexico, which is a safe third country where they could claim asylum, especially if they're coming from Venezuela or Afghanistan. So you have a population that overwhelmingly will not qualify under U.S. law for asylum. They're here because they want to get a job," he said.
But, critics say, taken together the administration's moves have gutted access to asylum.
Despite newly restored quiet along the southern border, the president's argument for the asylum ban has been rejected by two lower federal courts. It has, however, remained largely in place as the case is tied up in court battles.
In December, the Supreme Court will review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to adjudicate asylum claims, even as some of those countries face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the person seeking asylum won't be returned to their home nation.
The administration faces a third legal battle that could end its attempt to indefinitely detain thousands of people in deportation proceedings.
If the majority-conservative court rules in favor of immigrant advocates in the lawsuits, advocates say, the decisions could finally break the choke hold that the Trump administration has had on asylum approvals, which are at their lowest in decades. National asylum denial rates soared to 94% in June, up from about 50% in 2024 — the last full year of the Biden administration. That's according to TRAC, a research project at Syracuse University that tracks data about immigration judges.
"The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger," said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the Immigrants' Rights Project at the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the groups behind the challenge to the asylum ban. "The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court."
Lawyers for migrants seeking asylum are hoping for wins at the high court. For several of Madhavi Narayanan's clients, this could be lifesaving. A Los Angeles-based immigration attorney with Human Rights First, she is currently representing immigrants who, prior to Trump's second term, would have had what she calls "slam dunk" asylum petitions.
One of them is a 30-something Ethiopian man called ZG, who arrived in the U.S. through Mexico in February 2025 after enduring extensive torture in his native country. Narayanan requested that NPR use only ZG because he fears retribution from the Ethiopian government. Upon turning himself in at the southern border, ZG was placed into detention and immediately filed an asylum petition.
Narayanan said ZG is a member of an Indigenous group in Ethiopia that's part of an ongoing armed conflict in that nation, which human rights organizations report is at risk of committing more atrocities against civilians. And, Narayanan, who has been working on the case for nine months, said she has produced documents and letters to support his claims of torture.
"Any other time, it would have been a really straightforward case," she said, adding that "there's a wide, wide range of human rights reports explaining that folks in this exact position would be at high risk" of violence and death if they were to return to Ethiopia.
But instead of an immigration hearing, ZG was given a deportation order this month to Uganda, a country he has never set foot in and one that does not recognize the military violence in Ethiopia as a war.
In an effort to curb asylum applications and alleviate a crushing backlog of cases for U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the Trump administration is urging ICE attorneys to terminate asylum claims by convincing immigration judges that an application is incomplete or that a person can't substantiate their claims. Or the administration could argue what it did in ZG's case: that he could apply for asylum in a third country.
It has proved to be a highly successful strategy for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which has so far canceled thousands of pending cases.
Narayanan said experiences like ZG's reflect how Trump's changes to immigration courts have all but eliminated due process rights, including evidentiary hearings, clearing the way for summary removals. They also show how new guidelines are designed to limit a judge's autonomy. Recounting the events of the motion to end ZG's claim, Narayanan said the immigration judge told the court that his hands were tied.
"He was basically like, 'OK, I hear everything that you said, but I read this case and I'm not allowed to consider this,'" Narayanan recalled.
According to the Executive Office for Immigration Review, nearly 60 policy memorandums have been issued so far during the second Trump administration — a sharp increase when compared with the 30 immigration-court-related memorandums issued during Biden's four-year term.
The administration has also been aggressive in its pursuit to remake the immigration court bench, purging more than a hundred experienced immigration judges. Jennifer Peyton, a former assistant chief immigration judge in Chicago, told NPR that immigration courts across the country have become unrecognizable.
"Everything is different now," said Peyton, who was fired via email in July 2025 after more than nine years on the bench.
During Trump's first year back in office, nearly 40% of immigration judges were fired or resigned. Nearly all of them have been replaced with what the administration calls "deportation judges," who critics say are ideologically aligned with the president's immigration agenda and keen to rubber-stamp asylum denials and expedited removal orders. That shift, plus Trump's previous appointees, has overhauled the immigration bench. Now more than half of immigration judges are Trump appointees.
Of those new immigration judges, very few have experience working on behalf of migrants. About two-thirds of them come from a homeland security or military legal background, according to an essay in The Yale Law Journal by Geoffrey Heeren, an immigration law and policy professor at the University of Idaho. He wrote that "only about eleven of the new [immigration judges] have clear prior immigrant-defense experience, and of those, only one does not also have DHS or military legal experience."
In her previous role, Peyton was part of the immigration-judge hiring-and-training team with the Justice Department. She now practices immigration law representing asylum seekers and appears before the same judges she helped train. In those instances, Peyton said, she feels a bit more at ease because she knows the quality of the training they received. But when she argues cases in front of unfamiliar hires, she said, she's often dismayed.
"There is no doubt in my mind, when I have the misfortune to appear before them, that they don't know the immigration law so much and they don't care that they lack the training that we so rigorously put them through when I was on that team," Peyton said.
She added: "The vast majority have not been taught the process of evaluating a case, but rather the shortcuts to make sure that these procedural roadblocks come up, to make sure that the noncitizens are stripped of their due process."

How AI Impacts the Quest for Knowledge: Evidence from AlphaFold2

November 2026

ABSTRACT
Scientists can respond to artificial intelligence by pushing the frontier of science and asking new 
questions, or by deepening their understanding of questions already studied. We study how AI 
shapes this choice in structural biology, where experiments examine a protein's three-dimensional 
structure and its function. AlphaFold2, released in 2021, predicts the structure of almost every 
known protein, with a confidence that varies across proteins. Linking 530,471 proteins to the 
experiments run on them between 2017 and 2025, we compare how experimental activity changed 
after 2021 across proteins with more and less confident predictions. Where predictions are more 
confident, the experimental record adds fewer first structures for proteins far from any relative of 
known structure. It adds more follow-up experiments on proteins whose structure is already known, 
and the rise is largest for proteins surrounded by relatives of known structure. A model of 
experimental choice shows how AlphaFold2 can deepen existing knowledge rather than extend it: a 
prediction replaces an experiment that would establish a protein's structure, and it lowers the cost 
of experiments that build on that structure.
Myra Mohnen
University of Ottawa
Department of Economics
mmohnen@uottawa.ca
Joshua S. Gans
University of Toronto
Rotman School of Management
and NBER
joshua.gans@rotman.utoronto.ca
1 Introduction
Scientists can respond to artificial intelligence (AI) by pushing the frontier of science and asking
new questions, or by deepening their understanding of questions already studied. Both responses
are plausible. AI can combine scattered knowledge into predictions that open new questions
(Agrawal et al., 2019). But AI learns from past research, so it is most useful where scientists have
already looked (Hao et al., 2026; Hoelzemann et al., 2025). Which response dominates matters
because science is cumulative: what scientists study today determines what they can build on
tomorrow. Yet most work on AI in science asks how much it speeds up discovery (Aghion et
al., 2019; Cockburn et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023; Gao and Wang, 2024), not how it changes what
scientists study.
We consider how scientists’ choices responded to one of the most celebrated AI breakthroughs
in science, which came in structural biology. The field studies proteins, the molecules that carry
out most tasks in living cells. A protein’s three-dimensional structure governs its function and
underpins research on drugs and disease. Experiments determine a protein’s structure and show
how it works, for example, how it binds other molecules. Proteins with a common ancestor have
similar structures, so a known structure guides experiments on its relatives, and research clustered
around the few known structures: by 2016, fewer than 5 percent of the proteins we study had
one. In 2021, DeepMind released AlphaFold2 (AF2), which predicts the structure of almost every
known protein (Jumper et al., 2021), a breakthrough that earned two of its creators a share of the
2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Experiments continued, because a prediction is a hypothesis rather
than a measurement and does not show how a protein works (Terwilliger et al., 2024). But AF2’s
prediction can guide experiments as a known relative once did, even for proteins with no relative
of known structure. AF2 cast a light on unexplored proteins, but the light is uneven: AF2 is more
confident in its predictions for some proteins than for others. We use this variation to ask how
AF2 changed which experiments are worth running: which proteins scientists study, what their
experiments establish, and where those proteins lie relative to proteins of known structure.
Because AF2 removed the need for a known relative, experiments could have moved towards
unexplored proteins. We find the opposite: where AF2’s predictions are more confident, experi-
ments move from new proteins to proteins already studied. The experimental record gains fewer
first experiments, which determine a protein’s structure for the first time, and more follow-up
experiments on proteins whose structure is known (Table 1 defines the key terms). The more
confident the prediction, the more the experimental record deepens existing knowledge rather than
extending it.
We explain this response with a model of experimental choice adapted from Carnehl and
Schneider (2025). A laboratory chooses which protein to study and whether to determine its
structure or to study how it works. AF2 changes this choice through two forces that pull in opposite
directions. The first is substitution: AF2 supplies a predicted structure, so an experiment that would
determine it is worth less. The loss is larger for new proteins whose nearest known structures are
farther apart, where such an experiment would have been more valuable, so substitution pulls
2
research towards proteins already studied. The second is complementarity: AF2 provides a starting
point that lowers the cost of any experiment. The savings are also larger for proteins farther from
known structures, where existing structures offer a weaker starting point, so complementarity
pushes research towards the frontier. We show that the value lost outweighs the cost saved for an
experiment that determines a structure, because the cost saving arises for one protein while the lost
value spreads across related proteins. Far from any known structure, where nothing was usable
before an experiment, the balance depends on the prediction’s confidence. A prediction confident
enough to be used on its own makes the protein’s structure usable without an experiment, whereas
a less confident one makes a first experiment more worthwhile. An experiment that studies how a
protein works gains from complementarity alone.
We build a panel of 530,471 proteins from 2017 to 2025 and link each one to the experiments
recorded in the Protein Data Bank (PDB), the public archive of experimentally determined structures.
For each protein, we observe when it receives its first experiment and how many follow-up
experiments it receives afterwards. We classify each experiment by what it reveals: a structure
unlike any seen before, the first structure in a group of similar proteins, a small molecule bound to
the protein, the protein bound to a partner molecule (a complex), or an improvement on an earlier
structure. We place every protein on an evolutionary tree, which shows whether it is surrounded
by proteins of known structure, lies beyond them, or is far from any. A protein is a chain of amino
acids, and AF2 reports its confidence in the prediction for each one. We measure AF2’s confidence
in a protein by the share of its amino acids predicted confidently, which we call its AF coverage.
To separate AF2’s effect from other changes in structural biology after 2021, we compare how
experiments changed across proteins with different AF coverage, using a difference-in-differences
design with a continuous treatment. The estimates therefore measure how the response differs
across proteins, not a common effect of AF2 on all of them. Scientists could use AF2’s predictions
only after the code and a database of predictions were released in July 2021, and we hold each
protein’s coverage fixed across years. Coverage is not random, however. Proteins with low coverage
tend to be longer, embedded in cell membranes, and better studied, and they could have followed
different trends after 2021 for reasons unrelated to AF2. We therefore include year fixed effects
and protein or family fixed effects and let pre-release characteristics that capture scientific interest
and experimental difficulty follow their own trends after 2021. Before the release, experimental
activity shows no significant linear differential trend by coverage. Placebo estimates that randomly
reassign coverage across proteins, or move the release to 2016, show no comparable response in
total or follow-up experiments.
Moving from the bottom to the top quartile of AF coverage lowers the annual chance that a
protein far from any known structure receives its first experiment by about 0.16 percentage points,
close to half its pre-release rate of about 0.35 percent. Across all proteins without a known structure,
the decline is less than a third as large, about 0.05 percentage points against a pre-release rate
of 0.2 percent. Across all proteins, the same rise in coverage lowers experiments that provide
the first structure in a group of similar proteins by 24 percent. These are the experiments for

which substitution dominates. In contrast, follow-up experiments on proteins already studied rise
by 19 percent, and total experiments by 13 percent. Among follow-up experiments, complexes
rise by 26 percent, and improvements on earlier structures by 11 percent. For complexes, this
fits complementarity: a prediction of the protein alone can lower the cost of studying it with its
partners without showing how they fit together.
Where a protein lies relative to known structures shapes the response. Coverage raises ex-
periments most for proteins surrounded by known structures, and first experiments fall most for
proteins far from any. Among proteins surrounded by known structures, first experiments fall and
follow-up experiments rise more where those structures lie farther apart. The model explains these
gradients: AF2 makes it less worthwhile to determine the structures of the unexplored proteins
between known ones, and laboratories turn instead to the known structure nearby. The additional
follow-up experiments appear both on proteins a laboratory had studied before 2017 and on pro-
teins outside that earlier work. In proportional terms, they rise most where industry takes part,
in experiments whose last depositor works in industry and in those that combine academic and
industry affiliations. Academic laboratories, which deposit most follow-up experiments, show no
significant change in their total or follow-up experiments on average, but their first experiments
fall, and their follow-up experiments rise more where the known structures lie farther apart. Across
proteins and laboratories, AF2 concentrates experiments around existing structures rather than
extending them to unexplored proteins.
The response also matters because the knowledge it produces becomes part of what future AI
models learn from. Unlike commercial AI, such as a search engine, which improves as customers
use it (Farboodi and Veldkamp, 2026), AI models in science such as AF2 learn from new experiments
that scientists choose to run. Scientists choose experiments for their value to their own research,
not for their value as training data, so the release of one model can shape the data its successors
are trained on. This channel differs from the degradation of models trained on their own outputs
(Shumailov et al., 2024). Future models still learn from experiments, even when they also train
on predictions, and AF2 shapes that part of their training data indirectly by changing which
experiments scientists run. In our setting, the experiments that would extend future models to
unexplored proteins are the ones that fell, relative to other proteins, where AF2 is most confident.

Mullainathan and Rambachan, 2025). Three contemporaneous studies examine AF2. Hill and
Stein (2026) find that publications shifted towards proteins without a known structure, Qian

confident, and Sun et al. (2026) find that the long decline in the novelty of experiments stopped

protein and locate each protein relative to proteins of known structure. This separates first from
follow-up experiments, which move in opposite directions: first experiments fall where predictions
are confident, but follow-up experiments rise more, so total experiments rise.1

2 Protein Experiments and AlphaFold2
2.1 How Protein Structures Are Determined
Proteins carry out most of the chemical work in living cells. A protein is a chain of amino acids,
and the order of that chain is its sequence. The chain folds into a three-dimensional shape, the
protein’s structure, and that shape determines what the protein can do. Structures show where
another molecule can bind, how a mutation disrupts a protein’s function, and how a protein might
be redesigned. Most drugs work by binding to a protein, and structures of the HIV protease, for
example, allowed inhibitors to be designed against it (Wlodawer and Vondrasek, 1998). Structures
therefore matter for drug discovery, disease biology and synthetic biology.
While a sequence is straightforward to obtain, a structure is not. A sequence follows from the
DNA that encodes the protein, and public databases now list nearly 250 million proteins (The
UniProt Consortium, 2025). Until recently, a structure could not be reliably derived from the
sequence. It had to be determined experimentally, one protein at a time. We call a protein solved,
and Stein (2026) observe, because scientists can study a protein through its prediction without determining its structure.
Qian (2026) finds that experiments on well-predicted proteins fell by about 35 percent relative to less well-predicted
ones, concentrated in X-ray crystallography. We find instead that total experiments rise with coverage, because the
rise in follow-up experiments outweighs the fall in first experiments. Sun et al. (2026) compare post-release novelty
with the level its pre-release trend would have reached. Comparing proteins with different AF coverage, we find that
novel-structure experiments, defined against the structures available at each experiment’s release, show no detectable
response to coverage (Table 7), which is compatible with their finding. Within our sample, publications on well-predicted
unsolved proteins did not fall, and those on their structure rose (Appendix Table A3).
5
or say its structure is known, when it has at least one experimental structure associated with it.
Experimental structures exist for less than 0.1 percent of the proteins in these databases (RCSB
Protein Data Bank statistics). Human proteins are far better covered, yet even among them only
about a third had been solved in 2021 (Li and Buck, 2021).
Determining a structure experimentally is slow and costly, and it often fails. It requires purified
material, specialised equipment and trained scientists. Consequently, experiments are concentrated
in a few laboratories: before 2017, the top 1 percent of laboratories accounted for 31.4 percent of
experiments and the top 10 percent for 66.6 percent. There are three main experimental methods.
X-ray crystallography infers the arrangement of atoms from the way a protein crystal scatters
X-rays, so the protein must first be coaxed into a crystal, which many proteins never do. Cryo-
electron microscopy (cryo-EM) combines images of many frozen copies of the protein. Nuclear
magnetic resonance (NMR) uses measurements of atomic interactions to constrain the arrangement.
Historical records from the Protein Structure Initiative, an NIH structural-genomics programme,
illustrate the attrition and delays involved in experiments. Of the proteins it selected, 3 percent
ended in a solved structure. Those that did took a median of 1.4 years from target selection
to deposition in the PDB, and 2.8 years on average; 39 percent were deposited within a year of
selection. A single structure could cost on the order of $100,000 to $300,000 (Chandonia and Brenner,
2006; Terwilliger et al., 2009).
Proteins descended from a common ancestor often retain similar sequences and similar struc-
tures, so a solved relative can help determine the structure of a protein that has none. These
relationships can be represented as a tree whose branches trace descent from common ancestors, so
that the length of the path between two proteins measures how far their sequences have diverged
(Saitou and Nei, 1987). The closer a protein lies to a solved protein on this tree, the more that
structure reveals about its own (Chothia and Lesk, 1986). A solved relative supplies a starting
model, which scientists use both to predict a protein’s structure and to carry out the experiment
that determines it (Martí-Renom et al., 2000; McCoy et al., 2022). Before the HIV protease was
solved, for example, it was modelled from the protease of a related virus, and the model proved
close to the structure that the experiment later produced (Weber et al., 1989). Without a starting
model, an experiment needs additional measurements and costs more. Experiments are accordingly
concentrated where solved relatives already exist. Before 2017, the 1 percent of proteins in the
most-studied sequence clusters accounted for 34.5 percent of experiments; grouped by family in
Pfam, a database of protein families (Mistry et al., 2021), the top 1 percent accounted for 15.3 percent.
Solved proteins are also concentrated among human proteins and drug targets, and membrane
proteins, which are harder to determine, are underrepresented.
A protein can be the subject of many experiments. Among structures solved between 1995 and
2005 outside structural-genomics programmes, more than 70 percent of the structural units studied,
known as domains, came from proteins that had already been solved (Chandonia and Brenner,
2006). The HIV protease, for instance, has been the focus of hundreds of experiments that differ in
what they record. We call the protein’s basic three-dimensional shape, the folded chain on its own,
6
its scaffold. Some experiments extend the scaffold by resolving parts of the chain that no earlier
experiment did. Others capture the protein in a different shape, or conformation, as it closes around
a molecule. Others again record a small molecule bound to the protein, which we call a ligand; for
the HIV protease, the ligand is usually a candidate drug. A ligand that no earlier structure shows
bound to the protein is a new ligand. Others still capture the protein together with other proteins or
with DNA or RNA, which we call a complex, and a partner protein not seen with it before is a new
partner. Many proteins work only as part of such assemblies: a ribosomal protein, for example, is
solved together with dozens of other proteins and the RNA they bind, and the complex shows how
the parts fit and act together. An experimental structure can record any of these, whereas the AF2
predictions we use cover only the scaffold of a single protein.
2.2 What AF2 Added
Predicting a structure from a sequence became reliable in 2020, when AF2, a deep-learning system
built by DeepMind, reached near-experimental accuracy in the blind CASP14 assessment, a biennial
community benchmark (Jumper et al., 2021). DeepMind released the code in July 2021 and, with
EMBL-EBI, a database of predicted structures, the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (AFDB),
for about 350,000 proteins, including nearly the entire human proteome and the major model
organisms. In July 2022 the database expanded to more than 200 million proteins (Varadi et al.,
2022; EMBL-EBI, 2022).
AF2 predicts a structure mainly from the sequences of related proteins, which reveal which
parts of the chain lie close together, and, where available, from the experimental structure of a
related protein, although it can predict accurately without one (Jumper et al., 2021). It learned to do
so from the roughly 170,000 experimental structures released before 30 April 2018. Experimental
structures are therefore an important source of the model’s knowledge, though not its only one.
AF2 does not predict every protein, or every part of one, equally well. Each prediction reports a

ABSTRACT
Some social insurance programs, including the Medicare program in the United States, allow 
beneficiaries to choose between public and private insurance firms. In these types of programs, 
the government will often provide a voucher to those who opt for private firms. A key policy 
decision is the level of this voucher, and a key input to that decision is the elasticity of enrollment 
in the public versus the private option with respect to the size of the voucher. We estimate this 
elasticity in the Medicare program, where recent work has provided remarkably little evidence on 
how Medicare Advantage (MA) enrollment responds to payment despite the program’s rapid 
growth. We leverage the fact that the formula determining county-level “benchmark” payments 
(vouchers) involves coarse thresholds based on county-level spending and counties occasionally 
move across these thresholds, providing a shock to the vouchers unrelated to beneficiary demand. 
Using several complementary estimation strategies, we find that a 1 percent increase in a county’s 
benchmark raises MA enrollment by roughly half a percentage point within three years, implying 
an elasticity of about 2. Applying this estimate to a policy counterfactual that sets benchmarks at 
95 percent of county fee-for-service spending implies a decline in MA enrollment of about 6.1 
percentage points, or roughly one-quarter of our sample. We also provide suggestive evidence, 
consistent with prior work, that the increase in benchmarks gets passed through in the form of 
additional benefits, providing a mechanism for the enrollment increases

1 Introduction 
Many social health insurance programs allow beneficiaries to choose between a public option 
and provision of benefits by private firms. When program beneficiaries are given the option 
to opt out of public programs and instead enroll in private health insurance plans, the govern-
ment often provides some kind of “voucher” to those who opt out of the public option. In 
the United States, Medicare and Medicaid often consist of both public and private options, 
but other examples of public-private choice exist in Chile, Germany, and elsewhere (Vargas 
Bustamante and Méndez, 2016; Panthöfer, 2016). 
A key question facing program administrators is the amount of that voucher. A larger 
voucher results in more beneficiaries opting out of the public plan and thus lowering aggregate 
public plan costs, but it also results in higher program spending in the form of the vouchers.1 
Program administrators thus want to set the voucher where the marginal benefit of an extra 
dollar of voucher is equal to its marginal cost. The extent to which enrollment responds to the 
size of the voucher – the elasticity of demand with respect to the voucher – is thus a critical 
parameter for policymakers trying to determine the level of the voucher for two key reasons. 
First, it determines how many beneficiaries switch in response to a given voucher change, and 
therefore its net fiscal cost. Second, a strong enrollment response contradicts the idea that 
higher MA payments are purely a transfer to MA insurers, as an increase in enrollment implies 
that at a minimum some of the surplus was shared with the marginal MA enrollees to attract 
them to the program. 
In this paper, we estimate this parameter in one of the largest public-private health insur-
ance programs in the world: the US Medicare program. This program provides health insur-
ance to older adults and people with disabilities in the United States, and it has long been a 
pioneer of this type of joint public-private provision. The private arm of the program is known 
as Medicare Advantage (MA) in contrast to the public program, often referred to as Traditional 
Medicare (TM). 
MA payment works quite similarly to the type of voucher-based payment design described 
above. Under the MA payment architecture, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services 
(CMS) sets a county-level benchmark — the maximum government payment per enrollee — 
against which private plans submit bids. If MA plans bid higher than the benchmark,

externality is more relevant when the private plan is more of a “supplement” to a public option rather than a 
replacement (Palme et al. 2026). 
 
2 
beneficiaries must pay a premium to enroll. If plans bid below the benchmark, they are re-
quired to pass through most of the difference to the beneficiary in the form of additional 
benefits known as rebates, which may take the form of lower cost-sharing, supplemental ben-
efits like vision and dental, and reductions in mandatory Medicare premiums. A smaller por-
tion of any difference is passed back to the government. Thus, the benchmark behaves like a 
voucher. 
Despite extraordinary growth of MA enrollment over the last two decades, remarkably 
little is known about whether and how government payment generosity has driven this expan-
sion. Over the last two decades, MA enrollment has increased from a low of 19% in 2007 to 
a high of 55% in 2026, accounting for $462 billion, or 54 percent, of total federal Medicare 
spending in 2024 (Freed et al., 2026; Congressional Budget Office (CBO), 2024). Estimates 
suggest that payment relative to public program costs has fluctuated substantially, but in recent 
years, when much of the MA growth has occurred, MA payments grew at an annual rate of 
3.5% over 2013–23, compared with 2.6% for Traditional Medicare (Garrett et al., 2025). But 
are these two trends linked? Despite a large literature studying this program, there is remarka-
bly little evidence pointing to a non-zero elasticity of demand for MA with respect to the level 
of the benchmark. This makes it difficult for policymakers and the Congressional Budget Of-
fice (CBO) to make accurate predictions regarding proposed reforms to MA payment, either 
in the positive or negative direction (CBO, 2022). This has greatly limited the ability of poli-
cymakers to make legislation around MA, because the costs or savings of this legislation are 
difficult to model. 
Understanding how beneficiaries respond to voucher payments is also critical for evaluat-
ing the effectiveness of proposals that rely on insurer competition. In the MA context, it is 
not obvious that enrollees respond significantly to higher benchmark payments, as there is 
considerable evidence of inertia in health plan choice (Handel, 2013; Heiss et al., 2021) poten-
tially driven by information frictions or search costs. Further, MA plans are constrained in 
their ability to pass through higher benchmark payments in the form of lower premiums due 
to the zero-premium lower bound. Related evidence suggests that several non-pecuniary fac-
tors — such as perceived plan quality, provider network breadth, and brand recognition — 
may weigh as heavily as price in beneficiaries' coverage decisions (Rice et al., 2014), and that it 
may be increasingly costly to attract enrollees via these types of benefits due to their weaker 
salience and to satiation of consumer preferences on these dimensions (Stockley et al., 2014). 
Further, the MA market is highly concentrated, resulting in little pressure to pass higher pay-
ments through to enrollees leading to the possibility that insurers, instead of consumers, cap-
ture much of the surplus from higher benchmarks (Song et al., 2013; Cabral et al., 2018; Curto 
 
3 
et al., 2021; Pelech and Song, 2025). Further, payments may already be so high that there are 
few additional benefits that insurers can provide to newly entice beneficiaries to join MA. In 
other words, we may already be in the “flat of the curve” of the enrollment-payment relation-
ship. At the same time, it seems unlikely that large cuts to MA payment would not have any 
impact on enrollment. Yet, the current evidence base provides little guidance on this question. 
We seek to fill this gap by leveraging exogenous, intertemporal variation in county-level 
benchmark payment rates to identify the causal effect of government payments on MA enroll-
ment. Under the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act of 2010 (ACA), all U.S. counties 
are ranked every year into quartiles based on projected TM per capita spending, with the 
benchmark percentage declining from 115% to 95% as counties move from the lowest- to the 
highest-spending quartile. 
This formula generates plausibly exogenous changes over time through the annual re-
ranking of counties based on updated Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) spending projections. As 
a result of the yearly re-ranking, counties regularly cross these quartile thresholds and receive 
discrete payment changes unrelated to local demand for coverage or changes in underlying 
health needs. These changes are not transitory: 86.7% of counties that cross a threshold after 
2015 remain on the other side of it for at least three years. We exploit this persistence by 
identifying cohorts of counties that cross these payment thresholds over time and comparing 
their enrollment trajectories to those of counties that remain in their quartiles, identifying the 
causal effect of payment generosity on enrollment. 
Ultimately, we find that a 1 percent increase in the benchmark raises MA enrollment by 
about half a percentage point three years after the change, an elasticity of about 2 (2.1 in our 
preferred event-study specification; 95% confidence interval roughly 1.6 to 2.6). Event studies 
show that the enrollment effects of crossing the threshold occur precisely when payments 
increase, with little evidence of differential pre-trends between treatment and control counties. 
Enrollment effects were also approximately symmetric for positive versus negative payment 
shocks, further validating the design. These results are supported by several alternative speci-
fications including a simulated quartile crossing instrument constructed solely based on varia-
tion in national trends in FFS spending, a test for reverse causality, and an augmented synthetic 
control approach. Our key results are also supported by two separate placebo tests. The first 
examines counties whose benchmarks are capped, so that moving to a more generous quartile 
produces no increase in payment; the second examines counties that cross terciles of the FFS 
spending distribution instead of the quartiles used to set payment. Neither test shows an en-
rollment response. Further confirming our estimates, the results exhibit a dose-response rela-
tionship: counties experiencing above-median changes in their benchmark exhibit larger 
4 
effects than those experiencing below-median changes. In all cases, our results indicate a sig-
nificant enrollment response to benchmarks. 
Another contribution of our paper is examining how payment changes may translate into 
enrollment. We explore a range of potential explanations linking payment to enrollment, in-
cluding: changes in the value of additional benefits (through plan rebates), plan entry and exit, 
and premiums. Our event-study estimates show that benchmark crossings change average plan 
rebates by about $5.50 per enrollee per month and change the number of plans by roughly 
two plans in the direction of the crossing,2 consistent with insurers responding to payment 
changes through changes in benefits and market participation. When we split the results by 
direction of the crossing, the rebate response is driven almost entirely by benchmark increas-
ers, and the entry/exit response is driven mostly by plan exit in benchmark-decreasing coun-
ties. This suggests friction in adjusting benefits downward that insurers respond to with the 
extreme event of closing the plan altogether, producing similar enrollment effects to changes 
in benefits but via a different mechanism. 
In the last part of the paper, we explore the extent to which our results can help project 
how MA enrollment would change under an alternative policy scenario. Specifically, we use 
our elasticity estimate to simulate how MA enrollment would have changed during our period 
if payments were reduced to 95% of public program (Traditional Medicare) spending instead 
of the current estimated 107% (MedPAC, 2019). The simulation implies that payment reduc-
tions of this magnitude would reduce MA enrollment by about one quarter or 6.1 percentage 
points in our estimation sample. Thus, MA enrollment is responsive to payment, but this 
type of significant funding cut is unlikely to lead to the total demise of MA. 
These results fill a major gap in the literature on the Medicare Advantage program. Early 
work in the MA context exploited changes in payment rates in the Balanced Budget Act of 
1997 (Cawley et al., 2005) and discontinuities in the minimum payment floors for urban and 
rural counties (Duggan et al., 2016; Cabral et al., 2018) and found that enrollment generally 
responds to payment. More recent studies of the current benchmark system, however, have 
found little enrollment response to changes in payment (Schwartz et al., 2023; Murray et al., 
2024). Prior work leveraging county benchmark thresholds relied on cross-sectional bench-
mark variation generated by these thresholds, finding no association between payment varia-
tion and MA enrollment (Murray et al., 2024). However, that variation is potentially con-
founded by persistent differences across counties in provider market structure, beneficiary

Medicare Advantage program and the relevant components of the benchmark setting process; 
Section 3 discusses our empirical strategies; Section 4 describes the data and sample definition; 
Section 5 presents our results; Section 6 discusses the implications of our findings and con-

2 Background 
2.1 The Medicare Advantage Program 
Medicare Advantage is a publicly subsidized market in which private insurers offer managed 
care plans to Medicare beneficiaries — primarily adults aged 65 and older and those with long-
term disabilities — as an alternative to Traditional Medicare (TM). Insurers define the service 
area for each plan as a collection of counties, and beneficiaries may choose plans whose service 
area includes their county of residence. During the annual open enrollment period, beneficiar-
ies choose between TM, which imposes few restrictions on utilization or provider choice, and 
one of several MA plans, which typically offer supplemental benefits not covered by TM in 
exchange for prior authorization requirements and limited provider networks. 
2.2 MA Payment Policy 
Under the MA payment architecture, CMS sets a county-level benchmark representing the 
maximum per-enrollee payment the government will make to a plan operating in that county. 
The benchmark is determined by ranking all U.S. counties into quartiles based on projected 
per capita FFS spending and assigning each quartile a fixed percentage of underlying FFS costs 
— 115, 107.5, 100, and 95 percent, declining from the lowest- to highest-spending quartile. 
Plans in low-cost counties thus receive benchmarks that exceed local FFS costs, while plans 
in high-cost counties receive benchmarks below them. 
 
6 
Private plans submit bids reflecting their expected cost of providing the standard TM ben-
efit package. When a plan's bid is below the benchmark, it retains a share of the difference as 
a rebate, which must be returned to enrollees in the form of lower premiums for prescription 
drug coverage, reduced cost-sharing, or supplemental benefits — such as dental, vision, or 
hearing coverage. Because rebate dollars must by regulation be directed toward additional ben-
efits, the rebate serves as a direct measure of the magnitude of benefits provided to enrollees 
above and beyond the standard TM benefit package. When a plan bids above the benchmark, 
beneficiaries pay a monthly premium equal to the difference. In practice, the vast majority of 
MA plans bid below the benchmark, making the rebate channel the primary margin through 
which payment generosity reaches enrollees. 
Crucially for our identification strategy, quartile assignments are recalculated each year 
based on updated FFS spending projections. Counties whose projected spending crosses a 
quartile threshold receive a discrete change in their benchmark percentage, independent of any 
change in local demand for MA coverage or shifts in the underlying health of the population. 
These threshold crossings generate variation in payment generosity that is both plausibly ex-
ogenous and symmetric: a county whose FFS spending falls relative to a threshold may cross 
into a lower-spending quartile and receive a higher benchmark percentage, while a county 
whose spending rises may cross into a higher-spending quartile and experience a reduction in 
the benchmark. In our primary specifications, we estimate a single pooled effect of benchmark 
increases and decreases; however, we also test our hypothesis separately in each direction. 
2.3 Descriptive Evidence on Quartile Crossings 
Figure 1 reports the annual number of counties first crossing quartile thresholds between 2016 
and 2019, measured relative to each county's assigned quartile in 2015 and disaggregated by 
direction of crossing. Excluding counties that cross thresholds after 2019 yields a sample of 
2,370 counties over the 2015–2019 period, of which 1,115 (47.0 percent) experience at least 
one quartile crossing, with movements distributed roughly evenly between upward and down-
ward directions. This frequency ensures sufficient variation to support our empirical design 
while confirming that threshold crossings are a regular feature of the annual recalibration pro-
cess rather than isolated events.
